title: Moment-based approximation of cell and face integrals in THINC/QQ reconstruction on unstructured grids
summary: On unstructured grids, the tangent of hyperbola for interface capturing (THINC) method with quadratic surface representation and Gaussian quadrature (THINC/QQ) requires topology-dependent numerical quadrature for cell and face integrals and Newton iteration for the surface constant. This study introduces a quadratic moment-matched sigmoid (QMMS) approximation that evaluates these quantities from the mean and variance of the quadratic field while retaining the hyperbolic-tangent reconstruction profile and the boundary variation diminishing (BVD) formulation. A slope-matched Gaussian cumulative distribution function and a moment-matched Gaussian model provide closed form approximations for the surface constant and face averages, eliminating Newton iteration and topology-dependent runtime quadrature from these evaluations. Single-cell tests and nine two- and three-dimensional benchmarks assess reconstruction accuracy, flow-field differences, and computational cost. Across the tested cases, the principal transported and shock structures remain closely aligned with those obtained using THINC/QQ, with local differences concentrated mainly near discontinuities, contact regions, and developed shear layers. Reconstruction-stage profiling gives mean THINC/QQ-to-QMMS time ratios of 2.12 in two dimensions and 1.85 in three dimensions. QMMS therefore reduces reconstruction-stage cost while replacing topology-dependent runtime integral evaluation with a common moment-based formulation

AI.tldr: QMMS replaces THINC/QQ's Newton iteration and topology-dependent quadrature with a closed-form moment-based sigmoid approximation, matching accuracy while cutting reconstruction cost ~1.85–2.12×.
AI.motivation: THINC/QQ on unstructured grids is expensive: it needs topology-dependent numerical quadrature for cell/face integrals plus Newton iteration for the surface constant, limiting efficiency.
AI.method: Introduce a quadratic moment-matched sigmoid (QMMS) approximation computing quantities from mean and variance of the quadratic field, keeping the hyperbolic-tangent profile and BVD formulation. A slope-matched Gaussian CDF and moment-matched Gaussian model give closed-form surface constant and face averages, removing Newton iteration and runtime quadrature.
AI.result: Single-cell tests and nine 2D/3D benchmarks show transported/shock structures closely aligned with THINC/QQ, with local differences near discontinuities, contacts, and shear layers. Reconstruction-stage time ratios (THINC/QQ:QMMS) average 2.12 (2D) and 1.85 (3D).
AI.conclusion: QMMS reduces reconstruction-stage cost and replaces topology-dependent runtime integral evaluation with a common moment-based formulation.

title: An Approximate Method for Modeling Plasmons on Graphene with Time- and Space-dependent Properties
summary: This paper presents approximate computational methods for modeling surface plasmon propagation on a graphene sheet with time- and space-dependent material properties. Starting from Maxwell's equations, the evolution of current density under a spatially and temporally modulated Drude weight is formulated as a partial integro-differential equation (PIDE). Assuming small-amplitude perturbations of the Drude weight, a regular perturbation expansion is developed. The solvability and Fourier invertibility of the resulting order-by-order integral equations are established in appropriate Sobolev spaces. A numerical solver combining a Volterra integral equation formulation with the fast Fourier transform (FFT) is introduced, along with pointwise error estimates and computational complexity analysis. Additionally, an analytical transform-based solution using contour integration and Laplace inversion is derived for traveling-wave Drude weight modulations. Numerical simulations demonstrate diverse wave phenomena, including traveling, standing, and exponentially growing plasmonic current densities.

AI.tldr: Approximate computational methods model surface plasmon propagation on graphene with time- and space-dependent properties, formulated as a PIDE from Maxwell's equations, solved via perturbation, Volterra-FFT numerics, and analytic transforms.
AI.motivation: Graphene sheets with time- and space-dependent Drude weight require accurate modeling of surface plasmon propagation, which is challenging due to the resulting complex integro-differential dynamics.
AI.method: Starting from Maxwell's equations, current density evolution under a modulated Drude weight is cast as a PIDE. A regular perturbation expansion (small-amplitude regime) yields order-by-order integral equations with solvability and Fourier invertibility in Sobolev spaces. A solver combines Volterra integral formulation with FFT, with error estimates and complexity analysis. An analytic transform solution uses contour integration and Laplace inversion.
AI.result: Numerical simulations reveal diverse wave phenomena in plasmonic current densities: traveling, standing, and exponentially growing behaviors.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides solvable, efficient approximate methods for modulated graphene plasmonics, combining rigorous analysis, fast numerics, and analytical solutions.

title: An energy-based discontinuous Galerkin method for wave equations on complex geometric domains
summary: This paper develops a high-order cut energy-based discontinuous Galerkin (CutEDG) method for second-order acoustic wave equations on complex domains and across stationary material interfaces. The method employs unfitted Carte- sian meshes and addresses the small-cut-cell problem by introducing ghost-penalty stabilization directly into the local bilinear forms defining the EDG energy, while leaving the original spatial coupling and numerical-flux structure unchanged. We establish semidiscrete energy stability and a priori error estimates showing that high-order accuracy is retained. The formulation is further extended to interface problems with discontinuous wave speeds. Numerical experiments confirm the pre- dicted convergence rates and demonstrate robustness with respect to arbitrarily small cut cells. In particular, the explicit time-step restriction is governed by the background mesh size rather than the smallest physical cut cell, and the stabilized energy Gram matrices exhibit cut-independent conditioning.

AI.tldr: A high-order cut energy-based discontinuous Galerkin (CutEDG) method is developed for second-order acoustic wave equations on complex domains and across stationary material interfaces using unfitted Cartesian meshes.
AI.motivation: Solving second-order acoustic wave equations on complex domains and across stationary material interfaces is challenging on unfitted Cartesian meshes due to the small-cut-cell problem, which harms stability, conditioning, and time-step restrictions. The paper aims to retain high-order accuracy while robustly handling arbitrarily small cut cells without altering the original EDG spatial coupling and flux structure.
AI.method: The CutEDG method introduces ghost-penalty stabilization directly into the local bilinear forms that define the EDG energy, leaving the original spatial coupling and numerical-flux structure unchanged. It employs unfitted Cartesian meshes and is extended to interface problems with discontinuous wave speeds.
AI.result: The authors establish semidiscrete energy stability and a priori error estimates showing retained high-order accuracy. Numerical experiments confirm predicted convergence rates and demonstrate robustness to arbitrarily small cut cells: the explicit time-step restriction depends on the background mesh size rather than the smallest physical cut cell, and the stabilized energy Gram matrices exhibit cut-independent conditioning.
AI.conclusion: The CutEDG method provides a stable, high-order, and robust approach for acoustic wave equations on complex domains and across material interfaces, with cut-independent conditioning and time-step constraints governed by the background mesh.

title: The Mode of Null-A: Compositional Computation of a Generalized Inverse
summary:
We present a novel algorithm for calculating the preimage of an affine space through a product ${J}={J}_{T-1}\cdots{J}_0$ of matrices ${J}_t$ of special form: finding the largest input space $\mathbf{X}$ such that $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbf{X}$ implies ${J}\mathbf{x}\in \mathbf{Y}$, where $\mathbf{Y}$ is a given output affine space. These special matrices arise in AD, where the Jacobians $J$ describing the linearized computation have precisely this structure: the product of a series of linearized primitive numeric operations. This allows us to use the new algorithm to formulate Null-A mode preimage AD, which finds the affine preimage through the Jacobian or Jacobian transpose of a numeric computation. This is a generalization of the inverse AD problem of solving ${J}\acute{\mathbf{x}}^{\ast}=\acute{\mathbf{y}}^{\ast}$ or ${J}^{T}\grave{\mathbf{y}}^{\ast}=\grave{\mathbf{x}}^{\ast}$. The key is to represent affine spaces in a fashion which lends itself to efficient preimage calculation, in a compositional and quasi-local fashion, through a succession of matrices ${J}_t$.
  Unlike previous methods, Null-A preimage mode AD allows the ${J}_t$ matrices to be non-square, corresponding to a computer program whose number of active variables swells and shrinks during the computation. When ${J}$ is square and the initial affine space is a single point, this finds the conventional inverse. But in the more general case, having the entire affine space provides freedom which can be leveraged in a problem-specific manner. We apply the method to small problems on-CPU where the $J_t$ are linearized scalar unary or binary numeric functions; and to larger problems on-GPU where the $J_t$ are linearized aggregate array operations like convolution and attention.

AI.tldr: A novel algorithm computes the affine preimage through a product of special-form Jacobian matrices, enabling an extensible "Null-A preimage" reverse-mode AD that supports non-square Jacobians and computes the largest input affine space mapping into a given output affine space.
AI.motivation: Inverse AD typically solves linear systems Jx=y or J^T y=x, requiring square Jacobians and a single-point solution. The paper aims to generalize this by finding the entire affine preimage space through the Jacobian (or its transpose) of a numeric computation, which is needed when computations have varying numbers of active variables during evaluation.
AI.method: The method represents affine spaces in a compositional, quasi-local form that supports efficient preimage calculation through a succession of matrices J_t = J_{T-1}...J_0. This yields Null-A preimage-mode AD, which computes the largest input space X such that x in X implies Jx in Y, allowing non-square J_t matrices. It generalizes standard inverse AD and can be applied using linearized scalar unary/binary operations or aggregate array operations.
AI.result: When J is square and the initial affine space is a single point, the method recovers the conventional inverse. In more general cases, the full affine space provides freedom exploitable in a problem-specific manner. The method was validated on small on-CPU problems with scalar unary/binary linearized functions, and on larger on-GPU problems with array operations like convolution and attention.
AI.conclusion: Null-A preimage-mode AD generalizes inverse AD, handles non-square Jacobians arising from programs with variable active-variable counts, and returns the entire affine preimage space rather than a single point, which can be leveraged for problem-specific purposes.

title: The Ganglion Network Model: Evolving Trapped Phases in Porous Media
summary: Partially miscible ganglia trapped within porous media, spanning one or multiple pores and evolving through diffusive mass transfer, are common in subsurface (e.g., CO$_2$ and H$_2$ storage) and manufacturing (e.g., fuel cells) applications. We present the ganglion network model (GNM), a reduced-order method for simulating how a population of such ganglia evolves inside an arbitrary porous microstructure. GNM operates on a tree graph, the ganglion network, extracted from the pore-scale image of a given sample. Each point on the graph encodes a possible ganglion configuration in the void space, without any loss of geometric or topological complexity. The evolution of a population is modeled by representing each ganglion as a particle on the graph and tracking it according to a set of rules formulated herein. The rules capture capillary events such as pore invasion, retraction, snap-off, fragmentation, and merger. Unlike pore-network models, another graph-based modeling tool at the pore scale, GNM solves no system of equations and its cost scales with ganglion count, not domain size. We validate GNM against an image-based pore-network model in 2.5D and 3D domains with populations undergoing ripening, dissolution, and growth. We find good agreement in ganglion statistics, aggregate properties, and spatial configuration. We further argue that the ganglion network is the statistical space needed for extending kinetic theories of Ostwald ripening from single- to multi-pore ganglia, and provide an outline for how to do this. GNM opens the door to modeling other dynamics of trapped phases in porous media.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the ganglion network model (GNM), a reduced-order method for simulating populations of partially miscible ganglia in porous media using a tree graph representation, validated against image-based pore-network models.
AI.motivation: Partially miscible ganglia trapped in porous media are common in subsurface (CO2/H2 storage) and manufacturing (fuel cells) applications. Existing pore-scale modeling tools like pore-network models solve systems of equations with cost scaling with domain size, making them inefficient for tracking large populations of ganglia.
AI.method: GNM operates on a tree graph (ganglion network) extracted from pore-scale images of a sample. Each graph point encodes a possible ganglion configuration without losing geometric or topological complexity. Ganglia populations are modeled as particles on the graph, tracked via rules capturing capillary events: pore invasion, retraction, snap-off, fragmentation, and merger. Unlike pore-network models, GNM solves no system of equations, and its cost scales with ganglion count rather than domain size.
AI.result: GNM was validated against an image-based pore-network model in 2.5D and 3D domains with populations undergoing ripening, dissolution, and growth. Good agreement was found in ganglion statistics, aggregate properties, and spatial configuration.
AI.conclusion: The ganglion network represents the statistical space needed to extend kinetic theories of Ostwald ripening from single- to multi-pore ganglia, with an outline provided. GNM opens the door to modeling other dynamics of trapped phases in porous media.

title: Derivation of the Enskog--Enskog System from a Particle System
summary: We formally derive a coupled Enskog system for a gas--particle mixture from the hard-sphere BBGKY hierarchy. The derivation retains the finite separation between colliding centres, includes collisions within and between species and explicitly states the direction of spatial shifts and the mass-dependent prefactors of the four collision operators. The resulting system provides a kinetic starting point for two-phase flows for which the volume effect cannot be ignored. For unit contact factors, we derive the corresponding gas and particle balance laws, and establish an entropy inequality under suitable regularity assumptions.

AI.tldr: The paper rigorously derives a coupled Enskog kinetic system for a gas-particle mixture from the hard-sphere BBGKY hierarchy, preserving finite collisional separation and providing a kinetic foundation for volume-effect-dominated two-phase flows.
AI.motivation: Two-phase flows where volume effects cannot be ignored need a kinetic starting point; existing models often neglect finite separation between colliding centers, which the hard-sphere description can capture.
AI.method: Formal derivation from the hard-sphere BBGKY hierarchy, retaining finite colliding-center separation and including intra- and inter-species collisions, with explicit spatial shift directions and mass-dependent prefactors of the four collision operators.
AI.result: A coupled Enskog system for the gas-particle mixture is obtained; for unit contact factors, corresponding gas and particle balance laws are derived and an entropy inequality is established under suitable regularity assumptions.
AI.conclusion: The coupled Enskog system offers a rigorous kinetic foundation for two-phase flows with significant volume effects, exhibiting balance laws and an entropy inequality.

title: A Pre-trained Variational Autoencoder for Gyrokinetic Plasma Turbulence Surrogate Modeling
summary: Machine learning surrogate models offer a promising path toward accelerating plasma turbulence simulations. We present PreVAE-Turb, a surrogate modeling framework that leverages pre-trained variational autoencoders (VAEs) from the Stable Diffusion image generation model for efficient spatial compression of turbulence fields. The pre-trained VAE is fine-tuned on turbulence data using a physics-informed loss function that includes a spectral loss operating in Fourier space to enforce spectral accuracy across scales. The VAE is combined with convolutional long short-term memory (ConvLSTM) networks to learn temporal dynamics in latent space, with a manifold consistency error metric that monitors encode--decode consistency during autoregressive rollouts. We validate the framework on two-dimensional Hasegawa-Wakatani drift-wave turbulence and extend it to gyrokinetic turbulence from the GENE code, where a four-channel adaptation simultaneously predicts electrostatic potential, density, and parallel/perpendicular temperature fluctuations without requiring architecture redesign. Once trained, inference generates thousands of time steps in seconds on a single GPU, providing substantial computational acceleration compared to direct numerical simulation. The pre-trained approach offers a transferable methodology broadly applicable to various turbulence simulation codes.

AI.tldr: PreVAE-Turb is a surrogate framework that fine-tunes pre-trained Stable Diffusion VAEs with a physics-informed spectral loss and pairs them with ConvLSTM for latent-space temporal dynamics, accelerating plasma turbulence simulations.
AI.motivation: Direct numerical simulation of plasma turbulence is computationally expensive; surrogate models can accelerate it, and pre-trained generative models offer transferable compression without training from scratch.
AI.method: Leverages pre-trained VAEs from Stable Diffusion, fine-tuned on turbulence data with a physics-informed loss including a Fourier-space spectral loss. A ConvLSTM learns temporal dynamics in latent space, monitored by a manifold consistency error metric. A four-channel adaptation handles multi-field gyrokinetic data without redesign.
AI.result: Validated on 2D Hasegawa-Wakatani drift-wave turbulence and extended to GENE gyrokinetic turbulence, predicting potential, density, and parallel/perpendicular temperature fluctuations. Inference generates thousands of time steps in seconds on a single GPU.
AI.conclusion: The pre-trained approach provides substantial acceleration and a transferable methodology broadly applicable to various turbulence simulation codes.

title: Worst-Case Completion of Tensors with Approximately Few ANOVA Terms
summary: In this article, the problem of completing a tensor from some incomplete knowledge of its entries is treated by adopting a worst-case perspective, given the realistic assumption that the tensor's low-order ANOVA terms are dominant. We survey and leverage some recent all-purpose results from the field of Optimal Recovery to provide solutions on a theoretical level. But the accompanying constructions of optimal completion procedures, which often feature semidefinite programs, are not directly applicable in the tensor case due to the huge dimensions involved. To resolve the issue, we put forward a storage-friendly way to produce low-order ANOVA projections based on the fast Fourier transform (FFT), while exploiting the specificities of the completion problem to efficiently compute regularizers and extremal eigenvalues. Numerical experiments on synthetic tensors and real-world datasets demonstrate the accuracy and scalability of our FFT-based method.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses tensor completion from incomplete entries via a worst-case (Optimal Recovery) framework assuming dominant low-order ANOVA terms, and proposes an FFT-based, storage-friendly method to make the resulting optimal completion procedures scalable.
AI.motivation: Realistic tensors often have dominant low-order ANOVA terms, and tensor completion should be treated from a worst-case perspective. However, standard Optimal Recovery constructions (often semidefinite programs) are not directly applicable due to huge tensor dimensions.
AI.method: Adopts a worst-case Optimal Recovery perspective, leveraging recent all-purpose theoretical results. Proposes a storage-friendly way to compute low-order ANOVA projections based on the fast Fourier transform (FFT), while exploiting the problem's structure to efficiently compute regularizers and extremal eigenvalues.
AI.result: Numerical experiments on synthetic tensors and real-world datasets demonstrate the accuracy and scalability of the FFT-based method.
AI.conclusion: The FFT-based approach makes Optimal Recovery tensor completion practically feasible, achieving both accuracy and scalability for large tensors.

title: A Variance-Decomposition Formula for Direct and Adjoint Monte Carlo Particle Transport Problems
summary: In fixed-source Monte Carlo particle-transport problems, obtaining an acceptable variance on the sought response is of paramount importance. Currently, the only rigorous tool to analyze the variance of such games is the framework of the moment equations, which is unfortunately unwieldy to use in practice. In this paper, we establish a formula that enables expressing the variance of a Monte Carlo simulation as a sum of 'variance contributions' collected throughout the underlying particletransport process. This formula applies to both direct and adjoint games, and provides a new tool to pinpoint the variance-inducing mechanisms in Monte Carlo simulations, understand common variance-reduction techniques, and even conceive new ones. We showcase the use of the variance-decomposition formula on several applications. In particular, we revisit zero-variance schemes and analyze existing variance-reduction techniques, underlining their strengths and weaknesses. A few relevant numerical examples substantiate our theoretical findings.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a variance-decomposition formula that expresses the variance of fixed-source Monte Carlo particle-transport simulations as a sum of variance contributions collected along the transport process, offering a practical alternative to the unwieldy moment-equations framework.
AI.motivation: In fixed-source Monte Carlo particle-transport problems, achieving acceptable variance in the sought response is critical. The only rigorous existing tool, the moment-equations framework, is unwieldy and hard to use in practice, so a more tractable approach is needed.
AI.method: The authors derive a formula that decomposes the simulation variance into additive 'variance contributions' accumulated throughout the underlying particle-transport process. The formula applies to both direct and adjoint games.
AI.result: The decomposition formula is demonstrated on several applications: revisiting zero-variance schemes, analyzing existing variance-reduction techniques (highlighting their strengths and weaknesses), and supporting the theoretical findings with relevant numerical examples.
AI.conclusion: The variance-decomposition formula provides a new tool to pinpoint variance-inducing mechanisms, understand common variance-reduction techniques, and even conceive new ones, validated by numerical examples.

title: Global Solution Branches of Forced Nonlinearly Elastic Single-Director Surfaces
summary: We prove the existence of classical solutions for nonlinearly elastic, single-director surfaces or shells characterized by finite mid-plane strains and curvature. We employ topological methods, yielding solution continua far (in norm) from an unloaded, stress-free reference configuration, i.e., a global implicit function theorem of sorts. We first establish the existence of a local solution path, which is subsequently shown to be part of a global solution branch, viz., a maximal connected, locally compact set, emanating from the unloaded state.

AI.tldr: The paper proves existence of classical (global) solutions for nonlinearly elastic single-director shells with finite mid-plane strains and curvature, using topological methods to obtain global solution continua far from the stress-free reference configuration.
AI.motivation: Existing work tends to be limited to local solutions or linearized settings. The authors seek genuinely global solutions for nonlinearly elastic shells with finite strains and curvature, well away from the unloaded state.
AI.method: Topological methods are employed, effectively a global implicit function theorem. The authors first construct a local solution path, then extend it to a global solution branch—a maximal connected, locally compact set emanating from the unloaded, stress-free reference configuration.
AI.result: A local solution path is shown to belong to a global solution branch. Solution continua exist that are far (in norm) from the unloaded reference configuration.
AI.conclusion: Classical solutions exist globally for nonlinearly elastic single-director surfaces/shells with finite strains and curvature, providing a global branch of solutions rooted at the stress-free state.

title: Phase-Space Non-Integrability of Alpha Particles in Near-Omnigeneous Stellarators
summary: In a burning plasma, fusion-born alpha particles sustain the fusion reaction by heating the plasma core. Alpha-particle confinement in stellarators is sensitive to both deviations from omnigeneity and time-dependent Alfvénic perturbations. Traditional Poincaré maps rely on symmetry assumptions or dimensionality reductions that fail for stellarators with quasisymmetry (QS) error or multi-harmonic Alfvénic perturbations. To address these challenges, we investigate weighted Birkhoff averaging (WBA) as a diagnostic to detect the onset of chaos in guiding-centre trajectories subject to general magnetic perturbations. WBA exploits the super-convergence of time averages along quasiperiodic orbits, discriminating regular from chaotic trajectories using any smooth observable rather than an exact invariant of motion. Applying WBA to the canonical momentum $P_η$, we show that convergence tracks underlying orbit regularity even when quasisymmetry is imperfect and $P_η$ is not strictly conserved. Convergence is measured by the digit accuracy of the weighted average along guiding-centre orbits in fields with imperfect omnigeneity, with and without Alfvén eigenmodes computed using AE3D. We use this diagnostic to map phase-space chaos as a function of equilibrium invariants to identify transport barriers in unperturbed and perturbed stellarator equilibria. This work demonstrates that chaos induced by many Alfvén harmonics is often not apparent from the largest harmonic alone. We also find evidence that the onset of chaotic behaviour is sensitive to the local radial profile of the wave and not only to its amplitude at the resonance.

AI.tldr: This paper uses weighted Birkhoff averaging (WBA) as a diagnostic to detect the onset of chaos in guiding-centre trajectories of alpha particles in stellarators with imperfect omnigeneity and multi-harmonic Alfvénic perturbations.
AI.motivation: Alpha-particle confinement in stellarators is sensitive to deviations from omnigeneity and time-dependent Alfvénic perturbations, but traditional Poincaré maps fail for stellarators with quasisymmetry error or multi-harmonic perturbations due to symmetry assumptions or dimensionality reductions.
AI.method: The authors apply WBA to the canonical momentum, exploiting super-convergence of time averages along quasiperiodic orbits to distinguish regular from chaotic trajectories. Convergence is measured via digit accuracy in fields with imperfect omnigeneity, with and without Alfvén eigenmodes computed using AE3D.
AI.result: WBA convergence tracks orbit regularity even when quasisymmetry is imperfect and the canonical momentum is not strictly conserved. Chaos induced by many Alfvén harmonics is often not apparent from the largest harmonic alone. The onset of chaotic behavior is sensitive to the local radial profile of the wave, not only its amplitude at the resonance.
AI.conclusion: WBA provides a robust diagnostic for mapping phase-space chaos and identifying transport barriers in unperturbed and perturbed stellarator equilibria, showing that local wave profiles and combined harmonics matter for chaos onset.

title: A fully convergent fixed-point fast sweeping method with the WENO-JS local solver for steady state of hyperbolic conservation laws
summary: The fixed-point fast sweeping methods with weighted essentially non-oscillatory (WENO) local solvers are a class of efficient and high-order accuracy numerical methods for solving steady-state solutions of hyperbolic conservation laws. However, with the classical WENO-JS local solver, the iteration residue of high-order fixed-point fast sweeping scheme often has difficulty to settle down to round-off errors. To achieve the full convergence in a fast sweeping method, the fixed-point fast sweeping methods with non-traditional WENO local solvers based on unequal-sized substencils were designed. However, the WENO schemes based on unequal-sized stencils are more complex and in general more expensive in computational costs than the classical WENO-JS schemes. In this paper, we go back to the classical WENO-JS local solver and develop a new fully convergent fifth-order fixed-point fast sweeping method for solving steady-state problems of hyperbolic conservation laws. Based on recent studies on the nonlinear weighting process around discontinuities of solution, we apply the technique of frozen weights for avoiding unnecessary adjustment of nonlinear weights in the WENO-JS local solver, which freezes the nonlinear weights once the residual sequence in the fast sweeping iterations has stabilized. Different from the existing work on frozen weights, we design a simple and robust approach to judge stabilization of iteration residues and determine the iteration step when the nonlinear weights are frozen in the fast sweeping method. Extensive numerical experiments on a wide range of challenging two-dimensional steady-state problems demonstrate that, unlike the previous fast sweeping method with the fifth-order WENO-JS local solver, the proposed new scheme consistently drives the iteration residues to round-off errors and achieves the full convergence.

AI.tldr: A new fully convergent fifth-order fixed-point fast sweeping method is developed using the classical WENO-JS local solver with a frozen-weights technique to drive iteration residues to round-off errors.
AI.motivation: Fixed-point fast sweeping methods with WENO local solvers solve steady-state hyperbolic conservation laws, but the classical WENO-JS local solver struggles to settle iteration residues to round-off errors. Non-traditional WENO solvers based on unequal-sized stencils achieve full convergence, but they are more complex and computationally expensive than classical WENO-JS schemes.
AI.method: The authors return to the classical WENO-JS local solver and apply a frozen-weights technique that stops adjusting nonlinear weights once the fast sweeping iteration residual sequence stabilizes. A simple, robust approach is designed to judge stabilization of iteration residues and determine the iteration step at which nonlinear weights are frozen.
AI.result: Extensive numerical experiments on challenging two-dimensional steady-state problems show the proposed scheme consistently drives iteration residues to round-off errors, achieving full convergence unlike the previous fast sweeping method with the fifth-order WENO-JS local solver.
AI.conclusion: Returning to the classical WENO-JS local solver with a frozen-weights strategy yields a fully convergent, fifth-order, efficient fixed-point fast sweeping method without the complexity and cost of unequal-sized stencil WENO schemes.

title: MyTm: An Automated Melting Temperature Calculation Toolkit
summary: Melting temperature calculation is one of the important topics in computational materials science. In high-throughput in silico screening and artificial intelligence assisted design of materials, it usually requires a rapid and autonomous assessment of the melting temperature of the target. Unfortunately, molecular dynamics (MD) simulations of the melting point require many cumbersome and manual operations, making large-scale calculation of the melting point challenging. In this work, we introduce MyTm, a toolkit that employs MD to automatically determine the melting point. The method is fully modularized, and by combining these modules, the program enables fully automated melting calculations by using commonly adopted approaches, including the direct-heating method, the void method, the modified void method, the solid-liquid coexistence method, and the Z method. Moreover, a machine learning (ML) method is proposed and employed to recognize and classify the solid like and liquid like atoms, which effectively resolve the low accuracy issue in conventional classification approaches, thus making the automated high throughput pipeline of melting-point calculation possible. The robustness and efficacy of MyTm have been demonstrated by several well studied systems.

AI.tldr: MyTm is a modularized toolkit that automates molecular dynamics melting-point calculations by combining five common methods with a machine learning classifier for solid/liquid atom identification, enabling high-throughput screening.
AI.motivation: Melting temperature calculation is important in computational materials science, but high-throughput screening and AI-assisted materials design require rapid, autonomous melting-point assessment. Conventional MD simulations of melting points demand many cumbersome manual operations, making large-scale calculation challenging.
AI.method: MyTm uses MD to automatically determine melting points. It is fully modularized and supports fully automated calculations by combining modules for the direct-heating method, void method, modified void method, solid-liquid coexistence method, and Z method. A machine learning method is proposed to recognize and classify solid-like and liquid-like atoms, addressing the low accuracy of conventional classification approaches.
AI.result: The ML classification effectively resolves the low-accuracy issue in conventional classification, making an automated high-throughput melting-point calculation pipeline possible. The robustness and efficacy of MyTm were demonstrated on several well-studied systems.
AI.conclusion: MyTm enables fully automated, high-throughput melting-point calculation via modular MD methods plus ML-based solid/liquid atom classification, validated on well-studied systems.

title: Non Existence of the Stable 2D Boussinesq Equations in $H^2$ via Density-Vorticity Feedback
summary:
We establish instantaneous $H^2$ norm explosion for the two-dimensional Boussinesq equations around the linearly stable background profile $-x_2$. While previous ill-posedness results for this system relied on $L^\infty$-type spaces, this work provides the first strong ill-posedness result in the energy-critical space, where stable background stratification acts to suppress deformation growth.
  We adapt an idea from our previous work on the IPM equation \cite{BCMZ2025} and select an initial density perturbation vanishing near the origin to neutralize the stable stratification. Crucially, unlike the IPM setting, the evolution is here driven by the non-linear coupling between density and vorticity. Since the initial vorticity vanishes identically, the instantaneous loss of regulari\-ty is driven by density-vorticity feedback - a mechanism fundamentally distinct from both $H^1$ Euler ill-posedness of Bourgain \& Li and the IPM evolution.
  Through an iterative scheme yielding a sequence of approximations with strong deformation at the origin, we construct a strong solution $(ρ(t), ω(t))$ originating from data with arbitrarily small $H^2 \times (H^1\cap \dot H^{-1})$ norm, which immediately exhibits $H^2 \times H^1$ norm explosion for all $t > 0$ while maintaining uniqueness within the energy class.

AI.tldr: This paper proves instantaneous $H^2$ norm explosion for the 2D Boussinesq equations near the linearly stable profile $-x_2$, giving the first strong ill-posedness result in the energy-critical space, driven by density-vorticity feedback.
AI.motivation: Prior ill-posedness results for this system were confined to $L^\infty$-type spaces; the energy-critical regime remained open, where stable stratification suppresses deformation growth.
AI.method: Adapting an idea from their prior IPM work, the authors choose an initial density perturbation vanishing near the origin to neutralize stable stratification, then use an iterative scheme producing approximations with strong deformation at the origin; here evolution is driven by nonlinear density-vorticity coupling since initial vorticity vanishes.
AI.result: They construct a strong solution $(\rho(t),\omega(t))$ from data of arbitrarily small $H^2 \times (H^1\cap \dot H^{-1})$ norm that immediately exhibits $H^2 \times H^1$ norm explosion for all $t>0$, while retaining uniqueness in the energy class.
AI.conclusion: The work provides the first strong ill-posedness in the energy-critical space, revealing a density-vorticity feedback mechanism fundamentally distinct from $H^1$ Euler ill-posedness and IPM evolution.

title: FIREWALL: A surrogate model for the rapid assessment of tokamak wall loading and melting by runaway electrons
summary: Runaway electron (RE) beams generated during tokamak disruptions can deposit highly localized heat loads on plasma-facing components, posing a serious risk of melting and damage. Monte Carlo particle transport simulations coupled with three-dimensional thermomechanical response modeling can quantify this damage but are too computationally demanding for device-scale assessments and extensive scenario scans. We present FIREWALL (Fast Integrated Runaway Electron WALL loads), a surrogate model that combines a database of \textsc{Geant4} volumetric energy-deposition profiles with a one-dimensional heat-diffusion solver for each wall element. FIREWALL retains the energy and incident angle distributions of impacting REs and predicts the spatiotemporal temperature evolution of detailed three-dimensional wall geometries up to the melting threshold. FIREWALL thus provides a fast physics-based framework for translating global RE simulations into global wall melting predictions, enabling large-scale screening of disruption scenarios while directing high-fidelity costly workflows to the limited wall regions where they are actually required.

AI.tldr: FIREWALL is a fast surrogate model translating runaway electron impact into wall melting predictions by coupling a Geant4 energy-deposition database with a 1D heat-diffusion solver.
AI.motivation: Runaway electron beams from tokamak disruptions deposit localized heat that can melt plasma-facing components, but full Monte Carlo transport plus 3D thermomechanical modeling is too costly for device-scale screening.
AI.method: FIREWALL combines a database of Geant4 volumetric energy-deposition profiles with a one-dimensional heat-diffusion solver applied to each wall element, retaining RE energy and incident-angle distributions.
AI.result: It predicts spatiotemporal temperature evolution of detailed 3D wall geometries up to the melting threshold.
AI.conclusion: FIREWALL offers a fast physics-based framework for global wall melting predictions, enabling large-scale disruption scenario screening and directing costly high-fidelity workflows to critical wall regions.

title: A Kernel-Aware Two-Grid Preconditioner for Cell-Centered Nearly Incompressible Elasticity
summary: Nearly incompressible elasticity is often discretized by mixed methods to avoid locking, but the resulting saddle-point systems can be expensive to solve. We consider a weakly symmetric multipoint stress discretization whose stress and rotation unknowns can be eliminated independently over vertex interaction regions, leaving a symmetric positive definite system for cell-centered displacement only. Although smaller, the reduced system contains a parameter-dependent Schur complement that becomes difficult to precondition as the Lamé ratio increases. We show that its energy consists of a uniformly coercive shear part and a dominant semidefinite volumetric part. Standard cell-centered interpolation need not preserve the volumetric kernel and can introduce energy amplified near incompressibility. Motivated by this structure, we develop a two-grid preconditioner combining two complementary coarse subspaces: a conventional displacement subspace and a discrete-curl subspace lying exactly in the fine-grid volumetric kernel. Symmetric vertex-patch smoothing completes the displacement-only solver. The energy splitting and kernel-compatible decompositions yield a condition-number bound independent of the Lamé ratio for each fixed grid pair. Two- and three-dimensional experiments confirm the approximation properties of the locally eliminated discretization and show that the kernel correction prevents the deterioration of the displacement coarse subspace alone, also for discontinuous material coefficients.

AI.tldr: A two-grid preconditioner is developed for the displacement-only reduced system of a weakly symmetric multipoint stress discretization of nearly incompressible elasticity, using a displacement coarse subspace plus a discrete-curl subspace in the volumetric kernel to achieve Lamé-ratio-independent conditioning.
AI.motivation: Mixed methods avoid locking in nearly incompressible elasticity but yield expensive saddle-point systems. Eliminating stress and rotation unknowns gives a smaller SPD displacement-only system, yet its parameter-dependent Schur complement becomes hard to precondition as the Lamé ratio increases, and standard cell-centered interpolation may not preserve the volumetric kernel.
AI.method: Eliminate stress and rotation unknowns independently over vertex interaction regions to obtain an SPD cell-centered displacement system. Exploit an energy splitting into a uniformly coercive shear part and a dominant semidefinite volumetric part. Build a two-grid preconditioner from two coarse subspaces—a conventional displacement subspace and a discrete-curl subspace exactly in the fine-grid volumetric kernel—with symmetric vertex-patch smoothing.
AI.result: The energy splitting and kernel-compatible decompositions give a condition-number bound independent of the Lamé ratio for each fixed grid pair. 2D and 3D experiments confirm the approximation properties of the locally eliminated discretization and show that the kernel correction prevents deterioration of the displacement coarse subspace alone, including for discontinuous material coefficients.
AI.conclusion: The locally eliminated weakly symmetric multipoint stress discretization admits an efficient, robust displacement-only solver; augmenting the displacement coarse space with a discrete-curl kernel subspace yields Lamé-ratio-robust preconditioning for nearly incompressible elasticity.

title: SHIFT-Truck: A High-Fidelity Aerodynamics Dataset and Benchmark for Pickup Trucks
summary: Pickup trucks account for 14% of new light-duty vehicles produced in the United States, yet are among the least aerodynamic. Their open cargo bed adds a flow absent from existing automotive aerodynamics datasets such as DrivAerML and SHIFT-SUV: the shear layer leaving the cab roof passes over a recirculating bed flow before separating again at the tailgate. The resulting drag lowers fuel efficiency, raises emissions and limits the range of electric trucks. Scale-resolved Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) is too costly for broad design exploration; neural surrogates can predict flow features at a fraction of that cost, provided they are trained on large-scale, high-fidelity, domain-specific data. We introduce SHIFT-Truck, the first such dataset for pickup trucks. It comprises 1,000 Spalart-Allmaras delayed detached-eddy simulations (SA-DDES) of a reference pickup geometry morphed across 17 shape parameters. Each case is run on a mesh of about 100 million cells at a Reynolds number of $1.4 \times 10^7$ and released with time-averaged surface pressure, wall shear stress, volumetric pressure and velocity. The setup is verified by grid refinement and repeated runs, and checked against wind-tunnel measurements. We define geometry-grouped splits and benchmark four neural surrogates, DoMINO, GeoTransolver, AB-UPT and SMART, on surface and volume tracks. SHIFT-Truck also introduces controlled distribution shifts in the operating point, the input surface discretization and the vehicle archetype. Models with strong in-distribution performance can degrade substantially under these shifts: operating-condition changes expose failures to infer speed dependence, while tessellation and cross-vehicle shifts reveal markedly different robustness across architectures. SHIFT-Truck is thus a benchmark not only for surrogate accuracy but also for generalization across physical and numerical distributions.

AI.tldr: SHIFT-Truck is the first large-scale, high-fidelity pickup-truck aerodynamics dataset (1,000 SA-DDES cases, ~100M cells each, 17 shape parameters), with benchmarks for four neural surrogates and controlled distribution shifts.
AI.motivation: Pickup trucks are common but poorly aerodynamic, and their open cargo bed creates flow patterns absent from existing automotive CFD datasets. Scale-resolved CFD is too costly for design exploration, and neural surrogates need large, high-fidelity, domain-specific training data that did not previously exist for trucks.
AI.method: The authors built SHIFT-Truck: 1,000 Spalart-Allmaras delayed detached-eddy simulations of a reference pickup morphed across 17 shape parameters, each on ~100M-cell meshes at Re = 1.4×10^7. Data released includes time-averaged surface pressure, wall shear stress, and volumetric pressure/velocity. The setup is verified via grid refinement, repeated runs, and wind-tunnel comparison. Geometry-grouped splits are defined, and four neural surrogates (DoMINO, GeoTransolver, AB-UPT, SMART) are benchmarked on surface and volume tracks.

Models with strong in-distribution performance degrade substantially under these shifts: operating-condition changes expose failures to infer speed dependence, while tessellation and cross-vehicle shifts reveal markedly different robustness across architectures.
AI.conclusion: SHIFT-Truck serves as a benchmark not only for surrogate accuracy but also for generalization across physical and numerical distributions.

title: Magnetic Stabilization of the Greenhill Instability and Hysteretic Switching in Slender Rods
comment: This article is dedicated to the memory of Professor Robert V. Kohn, with respect and admiration. No generative AI tools were used in the development of the mathematical ideas, the derivation of the theoretical results, or the proofs. The authors are fully responsible for the content of the manuscript and for the accuracy, validity, and integrity of all results presented
summary:
In a bulk ferromagnet, magnetic energy is six orders of magnitude weaker than
  elastic energy. Slenderness removes this disparity. In a thin ferromagnetic rod, the two energies
  scale differently with aspect ratio, and an ordinary nickel wire deforms nonlinearly even
  under modest remote fields. We develop a three-dimensional variational theory of a
  ferromagnetic Kirchhoff rod under gravity and magnetic loading and study it through
  bifurcation analysis, computation, and experiment. A uniform field can stabilize a vertical rod
  against buckling under its own weight, the classical Greenhill instability. We give sharp
  criteria for clamped and pinned supports in terms of an Airy-type principal
  eigenvalue, and give a fine description of the character of the bifurcation landscape, which has qualitatively different features than its non-magnetic counterpart. When subject to the field generated by a
  permanent magnet, we identify a rich bifurcation landscape as the magnet is rotated quasistatically along a circle of radius slightly larger than the rest length of the rod. We prove that instability occurs only through a
  planar mode and that each snap is a nondegenerate saddle-node. We also locate the two
  folds that produce hysteresis.
  Experiments on $50\,μ$m nickel wires confirm the
  Greenhill threshold, restabilization at ~$30$ mT for both clamped and pinned supports, as well as the salient features of the hysteresis loop such as switching angles, width, and geometry of folds accurately.
  Our analysis and experiments offer principled design rules for field-stabilized filaments and remotely switched bistable
  actuators. Our analysis also offers a well-conditioned numerical method is valid near the switching events, where the direct numerical minimization is strongly ill-conditioned.

AI.motivation: In bulk ferromagnets magnetic energy is ~10^6 times weaker than elastic energy, but slenderness removes this disparity: in thin rods the two energies scale differently with aspect ratio, so an ordinary nickel wire deforms nonlinearly even under modest applied fields. This motivates a principled theory for field-stabilized filaments and remotely switched bistable actuators.
AI.method: A three-dimensional variational theory of a ferromagnetic Kirchhoff rod under gravity and magnetic loading, studied via bifurcation analysis, numerical computation, and experiment. Sharp stability criteria are derived via an Airy-type principal eigenvalue for clamped and pinned supports, plus a well-conditioned numerical method valid near switching events where direct energy minimization is ill-conditioned.
AI.result: A uniform field stabilizes a vertical rod against self-weight buckling (Greenhill instability). A rotating permanent-magnet field produces a rich bifurcation landscape; instability occurs only through a planar mode, each snap is a nondegenerate saddle-node, and two folds producing hysteresis are located. Experiments on 50 μm nickel wires confirm the Greenhill threshold, restabilization at ~30 mT for both clamped and pinned supports, and hysteresis features (switching angles, width, fold geometry).
AI.conclusion: The analysis and experiments provide design rules for field-stabilized filaments and remotely switched bistable actuators, and a well-conditioned numerical scheme for regimes near switching events.

title: A positive-conservative Fourier optimization method for ground states of Bose--Einstein condensates with higher-order interactions
summary: We develop a positive-conservative Fourier optimization (PCFO) method for computing ground states of Bose--Einstein condensates with higher-order interactions. The ground-state problem admits a convex density formulation, but the singular behavior near zero density poses difficulties for high-accuracy computation. We introduce convex regularizations of the density energy and establish their $Γ$-convergence on the computational domain as the regularization parameters vanish. The regularized problem is discretized by a Fourier pseudospectral method with mass conservation and nodal positivity. For the resulting constrained optimization problem, we use an accelerated first-order method for the main energy reduction, followed by a Newton refinement to reduce the remaining optimality residual. Numerical experiments show spectral-type convergence for regularized problems, quantify the effects of the regularization parameters on accuracy and spatial resolution, and demonstrate the effectiveness of the two-stage optimization method.

AI.tldr: A positive-conservative Fourier optimization (PCFO) method computes ground states of Bose–Einstein condensates with higher-order interactions via convex regularized density formulation, Fourier pseudospectral discretization, and two-stage optimization.
AI.motivation: The ground-state problem admits a convex density formulation, but singular behavior near zero density makes high-accuracy computation difficult.
AI.method: Introduce convex regularizations of the density energy with Γ-convergence as regularization parameters vanish. Discretize the regularized problem using a Fourier pseudospectral method with mass conservation and nodal positivity. Solve via an accelerated first-order method for main energy reduction, then a Newton refinement to reduce the optimality residual.
AI.result: Numerical experiments show spectral-type convergence for regularized problems, quantify regularization parameter effects on accuracy and spatial resolution, and demonstrate effectiveness of the two-stage optimization.
AI.conclusion: The PCFO method effectively computes BEC ground states with higher-order interactions, overcoming zero-density singularity via Γ-convergent regularizations.

title: Sign problem and criticality in world-line quantum Monte Carlo methods
summary: Discussions of the sign problem usually focus on its role as the primary limitation of the applicability of quantum Monte Carlo methods for reliably solving quantum many-body models. Its behavior as a function of spatial lattice size, doping, temperature, and interaction strengths has been carefully characterized within the determinant quantum Monte Carlo algorithm. Here, we consider the much less well-explored question of the temperature- and size-dependence of the sign problem in the world-line quantum Monte Carlo method. We review how, in this algorithm, even sampling the partition function of free fermions yields a sign problem, which we connect to non-analytic behavior in the corresponding reference model, hard-core bosons on a lattice. The latter exhibits a finite-temperature Kosterlitz-Thouless phase transition in 2D, and we show how this non-analytic behavior is imprinted on the average sign of the weights for the corresponding free fermion 2D tight-binding model. Our results thus show how phase-transition information can remain encoded in the sign problem even after direct sign sampling becomes impractical.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the temperature- and size-dependence of the sign problem in world-line quantum Monte Carlo, showing that even free fermions have a sign problem tied to non-analytic behavior in hard-core bosons, including a 2D finite-temperature Kosterlitz-Thouless transition imprinted on the average sign.
AI.motivation: The sign problem is usually viewed mainly as the key obstacle limiting quantum Monte Carlo for quantum many-body models, and its behavior has been well characterized in determinant quantum Monte Carlo. In contrast, its temperature- and size-dependence in world-line quantum Monte Carlo is much less explored.
AI.method: The authors examine the world-line quantum Monte Carlo algorithm, review how even sampling the free-fermion partition function produces a sign problem, and connect this to the reference model of hard-core bosons on a lattice. They analyze how non-analytic behavior, including the 2D finite-temperature Kosterlitz-Thouless transition, is imprinted on the average sign for the corresponding free-fermion 2D tight-binding model.
AI.result: Even sampling the free-fermion partition function yields a sign problem in world-line quantum Monte Carlo. The non-analytic behavior of hard-core bosons, including the finite-temperature Kosterlitz-Thouless transition in 2D, is imprinted on the average sign of the weights for the free-fermion 2D tight-binding model.
AI.conclusion: Phase-transition information can remain encoded in the sign problem even after direct sign sampling becomes impractical.

title: Quantitative homogenization and large-scale regularity for nondivergence-form equations under a critical ellipticity moment
summary: We prove quantitative homogenization estimates for linear elliptic equations in nondivergence form with stationary, symmetric coefficients, finite range of dependence, and a deterministic upper ellipticity bound. No deterministic positive lower bound is imposed. We assume that the reciprocal of the infimum of the smallest eigenvalue on a unit ball has a finite moment of order $d$, together with the common continuity condition of Armstrong and Smart. Under these assumptions, we obtain algebraic probability bounds for finite-cell errors and for Dirichlet homogenization errors with nonzero sources. We construct quadratic correctors on the whole space, modulo affine functions, and prove first- and second-order large-scale regularity and the corresponding Liouville theorems. We also identify the effective matrix through the invariant density and quantify smooth spatial averages of the density and the weighted coefficients. The proof separates a unit-trace diffusion from its physical clock. A reverse Hölder estimate for the Green function of a stopped coarse process yields the integrability gain needed to control the clock at the critical moment. Applications include weighted gradient convergence and a finite-domain approximation of the effective matrix.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes quantitative homogenization estimates for linear elliptic equations in nondivergence form with stationary symmetric coefficients, no deterministic lower ellipticity bound, and finite range of dependence.
AI.motivation: Classical homogenization for nondivergence-form equations typically requires a deterministic positive lower ellipticity bound. This work removes that assumption, handling degenerate coefficients via a moment condition on the reciprocal of the smallest eigenvalue.
AI.method: Under a finite d-th moment of the reciprocal infimum of the smallest eigenvalue on a unit ball plus the Armstrong-Smart continuity condition, the proof separates a unit-trace diffusion from its physical clock, using a reverse Hölder estimate for the Green function of a stopped coarse process to gain integrability for controlling the clock at the critical moment. Quadratic correctors on the whole space (modulo affine functions) and the effective matrix via the invariant density are constructed.
AI.result: The authors obtain algebraic probability bounds for finite-cell errors and Dirichlet homogenization errors with nonzero sources, prove first- and second-order large-scale regularity and Liouville theorems, and quantify smooth spatial averages of the density and weighted coefficients.
AI.conclusion: Applications include weighted gradient convergence and a finite-domain approximation of the effective matrix, extending quantitative homogenization to degenerate nondivergence-form settings without a deterministic lower bound.

title: Structure-preserving Fourier Neural Operators for Long-time Cahn-Hilliard Dynamics under Coarse Temporal Supervision
summary: Accurate long-time prediction of Cahn-Hilliard dynamics, particularly in the late-stage coarsening regime, is computationally demanding because it requires simulations over extended physical time. Various machine learning approaches have been developed to speed up the simulations through efficient surrogate evaluations. While the learned map can be accurate over a single learned interval, small prediction error will accumulate when the map is repeatedly applied in a long-time prediction, leading to large numerical errors. In this work, we identify the structure function for the coarsening dynamics of the Cahn-Hilliard equation and propose a two-stage structure-preserving Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) learning framework. Stage~I introduces a bound-conforming FNO (bcFNO) with a soft, magnitude-dependent amplitude penalty. Stage~II retains the bound-conforming objective and supplements it with structure-function regularization, yielding a structure-preserving FNO (spFNO) that corrects late-stage coarsening statistics. Numerical experiments on the various spatial resolutions and reference-solver time steps suggest that the bcFNO stabilizes the long-time prediction by suppressing large amplitude excursions, without changing the low online cost of the FNO. Furthermore, the structure-function term consistently reduces discrepancies in the normalized structure function and provides further correction in associated late-stage coarsening quantities, including the $L^3(t)$ growth trend and the scaling collapse. These results indicate that our multi-stage implementation of physical principles in operator learning could be applied to other multiscale systems with statistical scaling, such as the functionalized Cahn--Hilliard equations and turbulence, provided that the state constraints and statistical observables are adapted to the governing dynamics.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a two-stage structure-preserving Fourier Neural Operator framework (bcFNO + spFNO) to enable accurate long-time prediction of Cahn-Hilliard coarsening dynamics by suppressing amplitude excursions and correcting late-stage coarsening statistics.
AI.motivation: Long-time prediction of Cahn-Hilliard dynamics, especially in the late-stage coarsening regime, is computationally expensive due to the need for extended physical time simulations. While machine learning surrogates can be accurate over a single interval, small errors accumulate under repeated application, leading to large numerical errors in long-time prediction.
AI.method: The authors identify the structure function for Cahn-Hilliard coarsening dynamics and propose a two-stage structure-preserving FNO. Stage I introduces a bound-conforming FNO (bcFNO) with a soft, magnitude-dependent amplitude penalty. Stage II retains the bound-conforming objective, adds structure-function regularization, yielding a structure-preserving FNO (spFNO) that corrects late-stage coarsening statistics.
AI.result: Experiments across various spatial resolutions and reference-solver time steps show bcFNO stabilizes long-time prediction by suppressing large amplitude excursions while keeping low online FNO cost. The structure-function term consistently reduces discrepancies in the normalized structure function and further corrects late-stage coarsening quantities, including the L^3(t) growth trend and the scaling collapse.
AI.conclusion: This multi-stage implementation of physical principles in operator learning could generalize to other multiscale systems with statistical scaling, such as functionalized Cahn-Hilliard equations and turbulence, provided state constraints and statistical observables are adapted to the governing dynamics.

title: Well-posedness of the Stochastic Landau--Lifshitz--Baryakhtar Equation in $\mathbb{R}^d$
summary: This paper studies the Cauchy problem for the stochastic Landau--Lifshitz--Baryakhtar equation on $\mathbb{R}^d$, $d=1,2,3$, subject to Stratonovich Gaussian perturbations. We establish a low-regularity well-posedness theory for initial data in $\mathbb{L}^2$, $\mathbb{H}^1$, and $\mathbb{H}^2$. For $\mathbb{L}^2$ initial data, we prove the existence and pathwise uniqueness of global very weak solutions in dimensions one and two, while in dimension three we construct martingale very weak solutions on every finite time interval. For arbitrary $\mathbb{H}^1$ initial data, we prove the existence and uniqueness of global pathwise weak solutions in all dimensions $d\leq3$. Furthermore, for $\mathbb{H}^2$ initial data, we establish the existence and uniqueness of global pathwise strong solutions in the same range of dimensions. The analysis is based on a frequency-truncation approximation scheme combined with stochastic compactness arguments in the whole-space setting. The key step in global continuation is to justify the stochastic effective-field balance at $\mathbb{H}^1$ regularity, where the drift is available only in a negative Sobolev space. Spatial mollification and passage to the limit yield the energy identity for local weak solutions. A coercive modification then gives global energy moments and excludes finite-time blow-up.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a low-regularity well-posedness theory for the stochastic Landau–Lifshitz–Baryakhtar equation on R^d (d=1,2,3) with Stratonovich Gaussian noise, establishing global solutions for L^2, H^1, and H^2 initial data.
AI.motivation: The stochastic Landau–Lifshitz–Baryakhtar equation lacks a well-posedness theory at low regularity, especially in the whole-space setting. The challenge is that at H^1 regularity the drift term is only available in a negative Sobolev space, complicating global continuation and energy estimates.
AI.method: A frequency-truncation approximation scheme combined with stochastic compactness arguments. Global continuation relies on justifying the stochastic effective-field balance at H^1 regularity, using spatial mollification and passage to the limit to obtain the energy identity; a coercive modification then yields global energy moments and rules out finite-time blow-up.
AI.result: For L^2 data: global very weak solutions with pathwise uniqueness in d=1,2; martingale very weak solutions on finite intervals in d=3. For H^1 data: unique global pathwise weak solutions for all d≤3. For H^2 data: unique global pathwise strong solutions for all d≤3.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a unified low-regularity well-posedness framework for the stochastic Landau–Lifshitz–Baryakhtar equation across dimensions d≤3, with global existence and uniqueness established at the L^2, H^1, and H^2 levels.

title: Quantum Frozen--Oseen homotopy analysis method with LCHS for solving nonlinear partial differential equations
summary: Nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) underpin computational fluid dynamics, yet resolving nonlinear transport on fine grids remains computationally demanding. Quantum linear-evolution algorithms offer a possible route to large-scale simulation but cannot directly propagate nonlinear coupling. Here we develop a Frozen--Oseen quantum homotopy method (FOQHAM) framework that links transport-aware auxiliary-operator selection to the size of the resulting linear representation. We freeze the full Fréchet derivative at a prescribed flow profile, retaining transport and profile-gradient coupling and close each prescribed finite-order homotopy hierarchy as a fixed affine linear system by product lifting. We formulate its propagation through Linear Combinations of Hamiltonian Simulations (LCHS), without outer homotopy iterations or profile updates. For spatially semidiscrete equations, we establish local approximation bounds and exact closure of the finite-order hierarchy. Classical tests on Burgers, Korteweg--de Vries, Zakharov--Kuznetsov, and one- and two-dimensional isothermal compressible Navier--Stokes equations provide numerical evidence of accurate non-iterative approximations in the tested regimes. The framework thus connects nonlinear PDE approximation to quantum linear evolution and offers a conditional path toward quantum acceleration.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces FOQHAM, a Frozen-Oseen quantum homotopy method that converts nonlinear PDEs into fixed affine linear systems via product lifting and propagates them using Linear Combinations of Hamiltonian Simulations, enabling non-iterative quantum-friendly approximation of nonlinear transport.
AI.motivation: Nonlinear PDEs are central to computational fluid dynamics but are computationally demanding on fine grids. Quantum linear-evolution algorithms can handle large-scale simulation but cannot directly propagate nonlinear coupling.
AI.method: FOQHAM freezes the full Fréchet derivative at a prescribed flow profile, retaining transport and profile-gradient coupling, and closes each prescribed finite-order homotopy hierarchy as a fixed affine linear system by product lifting. Propagation is formulated through Linear Combinations of Hamiltonian Simulations (LCHS), with no outer homotopy iterations or profile updates.
AI.result: For spatially semidiscrete equations, the authors derive local approximation bounds and exact closure of the finite-order hierarchy. Tests on Burgers, Korteweg-de Vries, Zakharov-Kuznetsov, and 1D/2D isothermal compressible Navier-Stokes equations show accurate non-iterative approximations in the tested regimes.
AI.conclusion: The framework links nonlinear PDE approximation to quantum linear evolution, offering a conditional path toward quantum acceleration.

title: Computing electron overlap integrals for Gausslet orbitals on cubic lattices
summary: Gausslet orbitals on a cubic lattice, introduced in [Steven R. White, J. Chem. Phys. 147, 244102 (2017)], represent a localized, smooth, and systematically refineable basis set featuring a "diagonal" approximability of the electron repulsion integral tensor. The present work develops efficient algorithms for evaluating overlap integrals required for electronic-structure simulations using these Gausslets, specifically the kinetic, nuclear, and electron repulsion integrals (both with and without the diagonal approximation). Computational efficiency improvements rest on the exploitation of translation, permutation, and octahedral symmetries, a reordering and precomputation of nested sums, as well as an early truncation of small coefficients. Our algorithms reduce the number of electron repulsion integrals on a $5 \times 5 \times 5$ grid from $125^4 = 244140625$ to $324275$ due to symmetries, and achieve a wall-clock runtime for evaluating the remaining integrals with a truncation tolerance of $10^{-5}$ in under 2 seconds on a laptop computer. We apply the developed methodology to compute the ground state of the hydrogen atom and molecule as a demonstration.

AI.tldr: This work develops efficient algorithms for evaluating kinetic, nuclear, and electron repulsion integrals of Gausslet orbitals on a cubic lattice, exploiting symmetries, reordering, precomputation, and truncation to drastically reduce computational cost.
AI.motivation: Gausslet orbitals offer a localized, smooth, systematically refineable basis with "diagonal" approximability of the electron repulsion tensor, but efficient integral evaluation algorithms were needed to make electronic-structure simulations practical.
AI.method: Exploits translation, permutation, and octahedral symmetries; reorders and precomputes nested sums; and applies early truncation of small coefficients to evaluate overlap integrals (with and without the diagonal approximation).
AI.result: On a 5x5x5 grid, the number of electron repulsion integrals is reduced from 125^4 = 244,140,625 to 324,275 via symmetries, with remaining integrals evaluated at 10^-5 tolerance in under 2 seconds on a laptop.
AI.conclusion: The methodology is demonstrated by computing the ground state of the hydrogen atom and molecule, validating the efficiency of the approach.

title: Singular Sets and Doubling Properties in Parabolic Homogenization
summary: We study the singular sets of real-valued solutions to periodic parabolic equations with rapidly oscillating coefficients. Under a nondegeneracy condition on the corrector matrix, we obtain a local parabolic $n$-dimensional Hausdorff measure bound and a codimension-two Minkowski estimate. The Minkowski estimate holds at every scale, including scales below the oscillation scale $\varepsilon$, with a constant independent of $\varepsilon$. The bounds depend on a coarse-scale ratio of space-time $L^2$ mass to terminal-slice $L^2$ mass. Independently of corrector nondegeneracy, we prove that this ratio controls doubling at all smaller scales uniformly in $\varepsilon$. The singular-set argument combines summable errors in truncated Gaussian approximations, comparison of caloric polynomials at different time centers, and a stopping cover with microscopic singular-set estimates.

AI.tldr: Studies singular sets of solutions to periodic parabolic equations with rapidly oscillating coefficients; proves a codimension-two Minkowski estimate valid at all scales (including below the oscillation scale ε), with bounds depending on a coarse-scale mass ratio.
AI.motivation: Understanding the structure/size of singular sets of solutions to parabolic PDEs with rapidly oscillating (highly heterogeneous) coefficients, particularly whether estimates can be made uniform in the oscillation scale ε, including at scales below ε.
AI.method: Combines summable errors in truncated Gaussian approximations, comparison of caloric polynomials at different time centers, and a stopping cover with microscopic singular-set estimates; uses a coarse-scale ratio of space-time L² mass to terminal-slice L² mass.
AI.result: Under a nondegeneracy condition on the corrector matrix: a local parabolic n-dimensional Hausdorff measure bound and a codimension-two Minkowski estimate, holding at every scale (including below ε) with a constant independent of ε. Independently of corrector nondegeneracy: the mass ratio controls doubling at all smaller scales uniformly in ε.
AI.conclusion: Singular sets of such periodic parabolic equations satisfy codimension-two-type estimates that are uniform in the oscillation scale ε, and the coarse-scale mass ratio universally controls doubling behavior at smaller scales.

title: Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund inequalities for hemispherical $t$-designs
summary: In this paper, we introduce a new set of $\mathbb{L}_2$-orthogonal polynomials on the hemisphere $\mathbb{S}^d_+:=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d+1}:\|\mathbf{x}\|=1, \mathbf{x}\cdot\mathbf{e}_{d+1}\geq0\}$ and establish $\mathbb{L}_1$ Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund inequalities on the hemisphere for even and odd spherical polynomials. Hemispherical $t$-designs provide equal weight cubature rules on the hemisphere which are exact for polynomials up to degree $t$. We propose variational characterizations of hemispherical $t$-designs by the $\mathbb{L}_2$-orthogonal polynomials. Moreover, based on the Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund inequalities and the $\mathbb{L}_2$-orthogonal polynomials, we prove that for each $n\geq C_d t^d$, there exists a hemispherical $t$-design on the hemisphere with $n$ points, where $C_d$ is a constant depending only on $d$.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces new L2-orthogonal polynomials on the hemisphere, proves L1 Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund inequalities for spherical polynomials, gives variational characterizations of hemispherical t-designs, and shows existence of hemispherical t-designs with n points when n >= C_d t^d.
AI.motivation: Hemispherical t-designs provide equal-weight cubature rules on the hemisphere exact for polynomials up to degree t, but constructing them with prescribed cardinality requires suitable polynomial tools and inequalities. The paper aims to develop such tools via L2-orthogonal polynomials and Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund inequalities.
AI.method: Introduces a new set of L2-orthogonal polynomials on the hemisphere S^d_+, establishes L1 Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund inequalities for even and odd spherical polynomials, and proposes variational characterizations of hemispherical t-designs using these orthogonal polynomials.
AI.result: Proves L1 Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund inequalities on the hemisphere and, combining them with the L2-orthogonal polynomials, shows that for every n >= C_d t^d there exists a hemispherical t-design with n points, where C_d depends only on d.
AI.conclusion: The new orthogonal polynomials and Marcinkiewicz-Zygmund inequalities yield variational characterizations of hemispherical t-designs and guarantee their existence for sufficiently many points, with cardinality scaling like t^d.

title: Elasticity of polycrystalline davemaoite constrains its grain size in the lower mantle
summary: Earth's lower mantle hosts large low shear-velocity provinces (LLSVPs) beneath Africa and the Pacific, but their origin remains debated. Davemaoite, a major lower-mantle mineral, has been proposed as a contributor to these anomalies; however, its experimentally measured shear modulus is approximately 30% lower than first-principles predictions, a longstanding discrepancy between theory and experiment. Here, using million-atom machine-learning molecular dynamics simulations, we show that nanoscale grain-boundary disorder, invisible to conventional x-ray diffraction, can reconcile this gap. Introducing 5.8 vol% disordered regions reduces the shear and bulk moduli by 37% and 12%, respectively. This shear-selective softening can reproduce LLSVP-like seismic anomalies in basalt-rich assemblages, but only at disorder levels corresponding to grain sizes smaller than those expected in the lower mantle. Combining the disorder-elasticity relationship with seismic constraints, we derive a minimum davemaoite grain size of approximately 100 nm. This limit is consistent with mantle grain growth models and with attenuation-based evidence for coarse-grained LLSVPs.

AI.tldr: Nanoscale grain-boundary disorder in davemaoite resolves the theory-experiment shear modulus discrepancy, but only grain sizes below ~100 nm can produce LLSVP-like anomalies, which is finer than expected in the lower mantle.
AI.motivation: Earth's lower mantle contains large low shear-velocity provinces (LLSVPs) whose origin is debated. Davemaoite was proposed as a contributor, but its measured shear modulus is ~30% lower than first-principles predictions—a longstanding theory-experiment discrepancy needing explanation.

Introduced 5.8 vol% disordered regions and computed effects on shear and bulk moduli, then combined disorder-elasticity relations with seismic constraints.
AI.result: 5.8 vol% disorder reduces shear and bulk moduli by 37% and 12%. This shear-selective softening reproduces LLSVP-like anomalies in basalt-rich assemblages, but only at disorder levels implying grain sizes smaller than expected in the lower mantle. They derive a minimum davemaoite grain size of ~100 nm.
AI.conclusion: Grain-boundary disorder reconciles the theory-experiment discrepancy. The ~100 nm minimum grain size is consistent with mantle grain growth models and attenuation-based evidence for coarse-grained LLSVPs.

title: Stability of Kantorovich potentials via heat kernel regularization
comment: This is a survey paper submitted to the proceedings volume of the conference "18th MSJ-SI: Analysis, Geometry and Probability on Metric Measure Spaces - Fukuoka 2026"
summary: This survey presents heat kernel regularization as a method for quantitative stability of Kantorovich potentials for the quadratic transport cost. We give a complete new heat kernel proof on Heisenberg groups equipped with the Carnot--Carathéodory distance. For source densities bounded above and away from zero on bounded John domains, we obtain $L^2$ stability with rate $W_1^{1/2}$ for arbitrary targets in a fixed compact set, including atomic measures.
